Backdrop: IMF UK GDP 1.0% in 2026 rising to 1.3% in 2027; OECD 0.9% and 1.1%. Modest growth, not a demand shock. (3) GRANT THORNTON / UNIVERSITY OF LEEDS 'TALENT TRACK' (Consultancy.uk, 17 August 2026): a four-year accounting and finance professional degree, first cohort September 2026, multiple paid placements, a 15-month third-year placement, a permanent role with an ACA training agreement on completion, and stated plans to expand in following years. Source's position is unchanged and demand-positive - cautious-on-AI buyers down from 50% in 2025 to 23% in 2026, deployed-or-eager up from 15% to over 40%, technology consulting above $400bn in 2026 with growth rising to 7%. That argues for lowering the central estimate and narrowing the upper bound rather than the lower one. I hold the floor at 8 because four-plus years of model-capability uncertainty remains genuinely open and the credential-and-liability bundle is not provably safe to 2030. Central to 14, upper to 25.
forecasts.base_rate: The reference class is professional-services sectors losing a third or more of revenue or employment within roughly six years, with the loss primarily attributed by multiple credible analyses to a single technology. The class is thin and the closest members fit badly. Travel agencies shed 40-50% of US employment, but over roughly fifteen years, and the automated function was transactional booking rather than judgement. Legal document review contracted sharply but was a discrete commoditised task inside a larger sector, not a sector. Typesetting, photo processing, stenography and directory assistance collapsed faster, but each was a craft occupation whose single output a machine reproduced exactly. In every clean member of the class, the automated thing was the whole product. Economic consultancy fails that test structurally: clients buy a bundle of quantitative analysis, testimony admissible before a court or regulator, relationship capital with counsel and agencies, political and legal cover, insurable accountability and a credential that survives cross-examination. AI compresses the analysis layer, plausibly a third to a half of delivered hours and less of the fee. The remaining layers should appreciate as machine-generated analysis proliferates, because signing your name to a number before a tribunal is a liability transfer no model performs, and proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 would formalise exactly that asymmetry by holding machine-generated evidence offered without a human expert to full Rule 702 standards. Three adjustments push up. AI attacks the pyramid economics that fund senior capacity, with Big Four UK graduate intake down 6-29%, McKinsey cutting toward 40,000 from 45,000-plus, Accenture exiting 11,000-plus under an $865m charge and BCG entry-level down 15%. Pricing is decoupling from hours, which can deflate sector revenue without any demand loss. And the May 2026 Anthropic ($1.5bn, Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman) and OpenAI ($4bn-plus, TPG, Advent, Bain Capital, Brookfield) services joint ventures are the first credibly capitalised AI-native entrants aimed at the consulting pool. The adjustments pushing down have strengthened again. AI is itself a demand generator through compliance (EU AI Act high-risk obligations binding from 2 August 2026) and disputes (AI-related litigation filings surging in H1 2026); the AI consulting segment is growing roughly 21-24% a year from about $10.9bn in 2025; and the firms closest to the question are expanding, with CRA raising FY2026 revenue guidance to $805-820m and guiding to mid-single-digit headcount growth including a fresh university-hire cohort. There is also a hardening arithmetic constraint: a 33% fall from a 2024 baseline by end-2030, with 2025 and 2026 both growing, now requires a steeper annualised contraction across 2027-2030 than any published forecast contemplates. Scope decides a lot: read narrowly as CRA, NERA, Cornerstone, Brattle, Compass Lexecon and Frontier, current evidence points the wrong way entirely. Outside view 5-12%, adjusted to 13-17% for the AI trajectory and entry-level compression, then discounted for the demanding 'primarily attributed to AI' bar and the two-credible-analyses requirement. Central 14%.

forecasts.base_rate: The reference class is a governing party roughly three years from a required election, having changed leader mid-term, running level or fractionally ahead in a fragmented five-party system. Three anchors. First, incumbency plus seat efficiency, now quantified rather than asserted. Electoral Calculus on 28 July projected Lab 244 seats on 23.9 percent against Reform 127 on 23.4 percent and Con 132 on 19.7 percent, and put the probability of Labour being largest party at 58 percent. The premium is enormous at parity and evaporates within about four points, so the seat answer is very sensitive to small vote movements - the opposite of the prior's claim that a 1pp aggregate deficit barely matters. Second, mid-term leadership changes. Major 1990 and Johnson 2019 went on to win most seats; Brown 2007 and Sunak 2022 did not, a base rate near 50 percent, with the caveat that the winners went early while the honeymoon lasted. Ladbrokes prices an election in 2026 at 10/1, 2027 at 11/4, 2028 at 3/1 and 2029 or later at evens; an OLBG-reported version of the same market has 2026 at 13/2, 2027 at 7/1, 2028 at 2/1 and 2029 or later at 10/11, so roughly half the probability mass sits at the far end of the parliament. Right-of-centre fragmentation across Reform, the Conservatives and Restore Britain is the mechanism most likely to hand Labour a seat plurality on a historically low vote plurality. Two drags: governing parties in the mid-20s mid-term usually shed further ground once a Budget imposes real costs, with 28 October the first hard test; and prediction markets, reasonably calibrated on UK seat questions, sit at 35-40 percent for Labour most seats, well below this central.

forecasts.base_rate: The governing reference class is not 'blockbusters that reach $1.5B' but 'already-published box office milestones that are subsequently unpublished or restated below the threshold'. Theatrical cumulative grosses behave as monotonic series in practice: refunds, comps and currency effects are absorbed inside reported figures rather than clawed back from prior totals, and today's update is a textbook illustration, with the weekend-three estimate revised UPWARD by $1,000,000 (+1.43% on the frame, +0.05% on the cumulative) as estimates converted to actuals. Across the modern tracked-release era there is no recorded case of a major studio title's published worldwide cumulative being revised downward by anything approaching 26% after it cleared a round-number threshold. Routine revisions cluster in a 0.1%-2% band and arise from estimate-to-actual weekend corrections (rarely above 3% on a single frame, hence well under 1% of a $2.0B cumulative), currency retranslation of international grosses (a few percent on a territory, seldom more than 1%-2% on the global aggregate, and as likely up as down), and reclassification of re-releases or premium-format runs, material only for small titles. The largest genuinely contested restatements on record involve disputed territory reporting, most often China and India; even in the most-cited disputes the contested sums are tens of millions on billion-dollar films, i.e. low single digits in percentage terms. Here China is $197,600,000, about 9.8% of worldwide, and complete invalidation would still leave $1,825,232,000. The Rest of World residual, at $367,504,909, is 18.2% of worldwide and shrinking as territories are itemised; voiding it entirely still leaves $1,655,327,091. A second and now more salient reference class is source availability. The Numbers and Box Office Mojo have each operated continuously for over two decades, and the question resolves on either, so both would have to fail within a four-and-a-half-month window. However, the empirical evidence gathered over five consecutive checks is that Box Office Mojo's 2026 ingestion has been frozen since approximately 7 March 2026: its 2026 worldwide chart tops out at $614,786,686, its Spider-Man franchise page omits the film, and its release page returns no data. So the practical base rate to apply is closer to single-source than dual-source reliability. Even so, single-source failure at The Numbers over four and a half months, for a page that is updating daily and is corroborated by Comscore-fed trade reporting, sits at well under 1 in 1,000; combined with a sub-1-in-10,000 hazard of a 26%-plus downward restatement, residual failure probability stays comfortably below 0.1%.

The standing record is now approximately $105bn combined against a $70bn bar, so the required condition is survival of a 33% contraction rather than achievement of any growth, and that margin has widened materially in a single day. Firms compounding at these rates essentially never print an absolute run-rate decline absent a discrete shock such as product withdrawal, mass customer loss or an accounting restatement. Anthropic's documented path is now $9bn at end-2025, $14bn February, above $19bn March, above $30bn April, $47bn May, Q2 recognised revenue above $11.5bn with positive adjusted operating income, and above $65bn at end-July; OpenAI's is above $20bn at end-2025, roughly $25bn February, above $40bn per Bloomberg on 13 August with more than 20% month-on-month growth in July. A third class, and the actually binding one, is disclosure availability. NET REASONING. The arithmetic remains the question. Potential growth equals trend productivity plus trend labour input. On labour input, ONS 2024-based projections have natural change negative from 2026, net migration at 138,000 in 2026 stabilising at a long-run 230,000 from 2028, and the population up 2.3 million between 2025 and 2039 with migration accounting for essentially all of it: roughly 0.3 to 0.5 percent a year of working-age growth across the 2030s, with today's vacancy, payroll and pay data arguing the lower half of that if participation keeps slipping. On productivity, the anchors now bracket the threshold more widely than yesterday's write-up allowed. The pessimistic anchor is the outturn record: ONS series LZVD gives annual whole-economy output per hour growth of minus 0.4 percent in 2023, minus 0.8 percent in 2024 and plus 0.1 percent in 2025, and a decade mean of exactly 0.60 percent for both 2010 to 2019 and 2016 to 2025, with the index at 99.1 in Quarter 4 2025 against a 2023 base of 100. The optimistic anchor is the ONS-recommended RTI measure at 2.1 percent year on year. The official judgements sit between: OBR 1.0 percent, Bailey's 14 July 2026 Mansion House figure of about 1.25 percent, IMF potential 1.4 percent, Bank staff 0.3 to 0.4 percent per quarter in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report. Take 1.0 to 1.2 percent productivity plus 0.3 to 0.5 percent labour and potential lands at 1.3 to 1.7 percent, straddling the bar with the central point a shade under it. Then apply the shape of the question: a ten-year arithmetic mean is dragged asymmetrically by bad years, and a single minus 1.5 percent recession year subtracts about 0.3 points from the decade average on its own, while the 2030s carry non-trivial odds of at least one recession, energy shock, climate event or fiscal accident. That asymmetry, not the central potential estimate, is why this sits in the low thirties rather than near fifty. What changed today is the width and centre of the productivity input, not the structure: the strongest single negative in yesterday's file turned out to rest on the measure the ONS tells users not to use, and the AI capital build-out is now visible in official output and investment data rather than only in commissioned scenarios. Against that, three separate stress indicators, gilts, oil and labour demand, all moved the wrong way in twenty-four hours. One point up is the right size. The CI shifts up one point and keeps its 27-point width, since nothing resolved. The immediate tests are the delayed 18 August productivity flash, the 20 August Blue Book 2026 GDP impacts article, the 11 September monthly GDP print, the 17 September MPC, and the 28 October Budget forecast.
forecasts.base_rate: The naive outside view flatters the question. UK decade averages for annual real GDP growth were about 2.2 percent in the 1990s, 1.8 percent in the 2000s and 2.0 percent in the 2010s, with the 2020s running near 1.0 percent to date, so three of the last four decades cleared 1.5 percent and the unadjusted base rate is roughly 60 to 75 percent. That reference class is contaminated. Pre-2008 decades rested on labour productivity growth near 2 percent a year plus rapid labour force expansion from rising female participation and later EU accession migration; neither driver is available for the 2030s. The 2010s figure is itself misleading, resting on a deep post-crisis output gap that mechanically flattered measured growth through recovery rather than trend. Bailey's 14 July 2026 Mansion House speech makes the break explicit: potential supply growth averaged above 2.5 percent a year from 1990 to the financial crisis and halved to around 1.25 percent in the decade after it. The forward decomposition is the better anchor. Potential growth equals trend productivity plus trend labour input. The OBR cut underlying medium-term productivity growth to 1.0 percent a year from 1.3 percent in November 2025 and retained 1.0 percent in the March 2026 EFO, with further downgrades to growth in every year to 2030 trailed for the 28 October 2026 forecast. The IMF 2026 Article IV, concluded 16 July 2026, assessed UK potential growth at 1.4 percent. Bank staff estimates in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report put potential supply growth around 0.3 to 0.4 percent per quarter. Measured outturns are the weakest anchor of all: ONS series LZVD shows whole-economy output per hour growth of minus 0.4 percent in 2023, minus 0.8 percent in 2024 and plus 0.1 percent in 2025, with the index at 99.1 in Quarter 4 2025 on a 2023 equals 100 base, and decade means of 0.60 percent for both 2010 to 2019 and 2016 to 2025. Against that, the ONS now recommends users focus on its RTI-based estimate, which had output per hour 2.1 percent higher year on year in Quarter 1 2026 and 5.5 percent above the 2019 average. On labour supply, ONS 2024-based projections have natural change negative from 2026 onward, net migration falling to 138,000 in 2026 before stabilising at a long-run 230,000 from 2028, and the UK population growing 2.3 million between 2025 and 2039 with migration accounting for essentially all of it, implying working-age population growth of roughly 0.3 to 0.5 percent a year across the 2030s. Adding roughly 1.0 to 1.2 percent productivity to roughly 0.3 to 0.5 percent labour supply gives potential near 1.3 to 1.7 percent, with the central estimate marginally below the threshold. Shocks are asymmetric against the question: a decade arithmetic mean is dragged down far more by one recession year than lifted by one boom year, and medium-term official growth projections for OECD economies have systematically overshot outturns since 2008.
